title: Talk or build? Choosing the right format for group sessions
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli argues that leaders convening groups must choose between a focus group and a workshop by the kind of contribution they need: insight or progress. Focus groups surface perceptions, language and tensions, while workshops use structured exercises to produce shared outputs, alignment and buy-in. She gives examples (screening campaign, workplace culture, onboarding redesign), flags the risks of each, and offers do/don't lists. The leadership move is deliberate design of group sessions, and she notes the two can be sequenced. Close call with research methods; filed under Leadership because the operational target is facilitating groups of adults.
points: Choose the format by the contribution you need: understanding how people see an issue versus helping them shape a response.
Focus groups are for depth and diversity of language, not consensus; they are not a vote.
Workshops need structured, visible tasks and chunking to avoid drift and fatigue.
Workshops give both content and buy-in, but demand more from participants and the facilitator.
The two can be sequenced: focus group to find barriers, workshop to co-design responses.
quotes: What really sets these two methods apart is the kind of contribution you’re asking from participants. Focus groups are structured to surface insights: what people notice, value or question. Workshops are structured to generate progress: a shared framework, a set of options, a draft solution.
So: one format is geared toward learning from what people say; the other is geared toward what they make together.
There are risks, of course. Dominant personalities can skew the tone. Some people may self-censor, especially in hierarchical or sensitive contexts.
That shared shaping gives you both content and buy-in through a process of collaborative co-creation.
Done well, a workshop can generate clarity and alignment that would take weeks to build through interviews or surveys. Done poorly, it becomes a group activity with no real traction.
Don’t call something a workshop if you’re just hosting a longer group discussion. Don’t label something a focus group if you’re asking people to generate ideas or solutions.
